description: my name is mohammed ali alfahdi the team leader and a games developer . our challenge statment: Space Mission Design Game: create an interactive game in which players design, manage and simulate a complete space mission (objectives, spacecraft and instruments, launch vehicle, budget, power, mass, communications and orbit), making engineering decisions with limited resources and seeing how each choice affects the mission's success.
summary: What if a real NASA satellite image decided whether your mission works? Majan Mission is a first-person 3D game, in Arabic and English, that runs in any web browser. The player runs Oman's space center and takes an Earth-observation satellite from a contract to orbit: buys parts and fits them by hand in the clean room, chooses the orbit, instruments, power, antenna, ground stations, tests, end-of-mission plan and rocket under a fixed budget, passes a design review, launches from Duqm and handles events taken from real missions. Six live meters show how each choice changes cost, mass, power and data, and every mission has more than one good design. The three missions answer needs in Oman: mapping the aflaj water channels, watching the Khareef monsoon clouds, tracking the dunes of the Sharqiya Sands. The cloud cover in the rules is measured in NASA MODIS images, saved in the game or fetched live for any day since 2000, so the sky NASA recorded decides whether a camera or a radar is the better instrument. A science page recomputes 22 checks in the visitor's own browser. It matters because students rarely make these trade-offs themselves, and there is very little interactive space content in Arabic.
details:
Short on time? Three links

  • Play in two minutes: https://maahf1.github.io/majan-mission-game/center.html?judge=1&lang=en opens Mission Control with a satellite ready for the Khareef mission. Change a decision, watch the meters, press Launch.
  • Check the science yourself: https://maahf1.github.io/majan-mission-game/science.html runs 22 checks in your browser.
  • Watch: a two-minute walkthrough, https://maahf1.github.io/majan-mission-game/demo/majan-walkthrough.mp4

Full game: https://maahf1.github.io/majan-mission-game/center.html?lang=en (laptop or phone, no login). Code: https://github.com/maahf1/majan-mission-game

The problem

Oman is building a space sector: a National Space Policy and Executive Programme (2023 to 2033), the Etlaq spaceport in Duqm, and a Space Settlement Centre planned beside it. It will need people who can design missions. Students hear about it, but they rarely get to make a mission's trade-offs themselves, and there is very little interactive space content in Arabic.

What Majan Mission is

A first-person 3D game in the browser, in Arabic and English. The player runs Oman's space center and flies three missions about real needs in Oman: mapping the aflaj water channels, watching the Khareef monsoon clouds over Dhofar, and tracking the moving dunes of the Sharqiya Sands. A mission is five steps, each at its own place in the center: choose a contract, build the satellite by hand, design the mission and pass a review, launch from Duqm, and operate in orbit.

What makes it different

A NASA image is a rule, not a picture on the wall. The game counts the cloud in NASA's MODIS image of each target, pixel by pixel. On 10 August 2024, 49.5% of the Dhofar scene was under cloud, so in the Khareef mission a camera that looks at the ground loses 49.5% of its images, radar loses none, and the wide-view and thermal cameras watch the clouds themselves. The sky NASA recorded decides which instrument is right.

The sky is live. The player can pick yesterday, or any day since 2000. The browser asks NASA GIBS for that day's MODIS Terra image of the target and measures the cloud on the spot; instrument fit, the forecast and the mission change with it. With no internet, the saved image stays in use.

The science can be checked by anyone. https://maahf1.github.io/majan-mission-game/science.html recomputes its checks each time it opens, from the same rules the game plays with: the three orbit periods against Kepler's third law; the same formula against the periods NASA publishes for Landsat 9, Terra, SMAP, GPM and Sentinel-6; sunlight in each orbit against the geometry of Earth's shadow; the cloud cover, measured again in NASA's images; and every design the game allows, built one by one (61,236 designs; of the 8,585 that may launch, none breaks the 25-year disposal rule, the mass limit or the budget). Each mission has 19 to 27 three-star designs in two or three orbits, so there is no single right answer. The numbers are simplified for teaching, and the page shows how far each is from the physics.

The player is inside the building. Parts are ordered, delivered by truck, carried and fitted by hand before the player sits down at Mission Control.

How the simulation works

  • Power: panels work only in sunlight (62% to 72% of an orbit). If the equipment uses more than they make, the battery drains in shadow and the mission ends early.
  • Data: only what the antenna and the ground stations can take reaches Oman; a sharp camera with a weak antenna fills a backlog.
  • Mass: every part adds mass, and a higher orbit lowers what each rocket can lift.
  • Orbit: low orbits give sharper images but decay in about two years; high orbits see more but would leave debris for centuries.
  • Disposal: no launch unless the satellite leaves orbit within 25 years of its mission (NASA-STD-8719.14), by decay, a drag sail or a thruster.
  • Testing: skipping tests raises the chance of an early fault.

The design review

Before launch, six requirements are verified, the design climbs a four-level concept maturity ladder, a trade study plots it against a large sample of other designs (science against cost), and a "real missions" tab sets it beside the closest missions of NASA and its partners.

In orbit, and after

Events come from real missions: the solar storms of October 2003, the units mix-up that lost Mars Climate Orbiter, debris avoidance, a busy ground station. The results give one to three stars and a plain-language line for each cause. A mission report with NASA images of the target can be saved as a PDF.

Built for a classroom

Up to four students share one mission on one device, as mission planner, spacecraft engineer, science lead and communications lead. A short quiz before and after shows the change in score. A mission fits a lesson (15 to 20 minutes), runs on school laptops and phones, in Arabic or English, and works with no internet from a copy on the school's computer.

The Duqm Space Settlement

Outside the center stands our own 3D model of a settlement, inspired by the Space Settlement Centre planned in Duqm to rehearse life on the Moon and Mars. Stars earned in missions build it: a greenhouse at two stars, a solar field at four, a research building at six, a landing pad at nine. A notice board explains the real project. It is the team's model, not the official design.

How the game answers the challenge

Every item the challenge names is a decision in the game: objectives (three contracts), spacecraft and instruments (six instrument types, two bays), launch vehicle (three rockets), budget, power, mass, communications (three antennas, three ground-station options) and orbits (400, 700 and 1,200 km). The mission is then flown hour by hour, and the results explain how each choice shaped the outcome. Every NASA resource listed for the challenge has a place in the game.

We are an engineer, two computer science teachers and an English teacher. We chose the Space Mission Design Game because we teach students who have very little interactive space content in Arabic, and we set the game in Oman so they could plan a mission for places they know.

Tested, and what comes next

An automated player (Playwright driving Chrome) plays a whole mission from the office to the results, in English and Arabic, on the published site. A balance tool builds every design. The game was also run with all outside connections blocked. Next: a classroom pilot in Ibra with the built-in quiz, more missions (a Moon lander, a Mars orbiter), and open code so other teams can add missions for their own countries.

Tools: JavaScript (ES modules), Three.js 0.160, HTML and CSS; Blender 5.2 with Python for the 3D models; Node.js, Playwright and Chrome for tests; ffmpeg for the videos; PowerPoint for the pitch deck.

More to see: the quick design mode, the same rules on one screen, https://maahf1.github.io/majan-mission-game/index.html?lang=en

Expert feedback

Eng. Bahiya bint Hilal Al Shuaibi, founder and CEO of Global Space and Technology Company (Oman), told the team on 14 November 2026 (translated from Arabic): "The idea of Majan Mission is distinctive, and it mirrors an important part of real space mission engineering, especially the balance between budget, power, orbit and science instruments. Games like this also help simulate realistic scenarios and build decision-making and a quick response to unexpected challenges, which prepares students for practical experience later."

Use of artificial intelligence

We used Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, as an assistant.

  • Ideas and research: brainstorming features, and finding and summarising public NASA sources; we decided what went into the game.
  • Code: it wrote most of the game code under our direction, including the live NASA sky and the science check page; we play-tested each version and decided what to keep.
  • Data analysis: code written with the assistant measures the cloud cover in NASA MODIS images; the game uses the values as a rule.
  • 3D models: the satellite's body and solar array are NASA's 3D model of Landsat 8 (NASA 3D Resources), re-coloured by a script. Everything else is generated by Blender and JavaScript code written with the assistant.
  • Visual design: screen layouts, 3D scenes, slides and the pictures on this page were made with the assistant. The pictures here are real screenshots of the game and real NASA images, arranged with captions. No image generator was used.
  • Video: the demo and the walkthrough are real captures of the game; the recording script and the short synthesized soundtrack were written with the assistant. Each video carries a visible note saying so.
  • Text: drafting and translation between Arabic and English, including this page.
  • Not AI-generated: the satellite images are real NASA data. No NASA logo or branding was generated or used.
